title: The greeting to the dead
hook: peace upon you, people of these dwellings (Muslim)
carry: peace upon you, people of the graves

segments.voice: Yesterday, visiting graves: once forbidden, then opened, because they remind. Your line: they remind. Did you pass a cemetery, or plan a visit? Today, what you say when you get there. Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

It's night in Madinah, and 'A'ishah is awake when her husband gets up. In a long hadith in Sahih Muslim, she tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, slipped out quietly, and she followed him through the dark. He went to al-Baqi', the graveyard. He stood there a long time, raised his hands three times, and then turned back. She hurried home ahead of him, out of breath, and he asked what was wrong. It all came out. And when it had, she asked him the question underneath it: what should I say to them, when I go there?
screen: `NIGHT IN MADINAH.` → `HE GOES TO AL-BAQI'.` → `WHAT SHOULD I SAY TO THEM?`

segments.voice: He told her. And in another report in Sahih Muslim, from Buraydah, he taught the same words to his companions whenever they went out to the graves. They begin: as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar. Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings. Then, in paraphrase, the greeting goes on: you who are believers and Muslims, and we, if God wills, will be joining you. And it asks God for well-being, for us and for you. Sit with how strange and how tender that is. As-salamu 'alaykum is the greeting Muslims give the living: at the door, in the street, at the close of the prayer. Here it's said to the dead, in the same words. No special voice for a cemetery. The dead are greeted the way you'd greet a neighbor. And look at what the graves are called. Not holes, not plots. Dwellings. Homes. The people buried there are residents, and you're a visitor in their neighborhood. Then the honest middle line: we will be joining you. Nobody pretends otherwise. The visitor and the visited are on the same road, just at different points along it. And the last line asks for well-being for both at once: for us, and for you. The living don't stand above the dead, praying down at them. They stand beside them and ask together. In 'A'ishah's version the Prophet also asks for mercy on those who have gone ahead and those who come later. One greeting, and the whole line of people, before and after, is inside it.
screen: `AS-SALAMU 'ALAYKUM, AHL AD-DIYAR.` · `THE SAME GREETING AS THE LIVING.` · `WE WILL BE JOINING YOU.` · `FOR US, AND FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn the greeting. Settle and breathe. Say the opening quietly, a few times, until it sits easily: as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar. Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings. Then think of a graveyard you know, and the people resting there, named or unnamed. If you pray, you can offer them the greeting, the way it was taught. If not, simply hold them in mind, as neighbors on the same road. Let the words settle between breaths. The bell holds the time.
The greeting to the dead. Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings: the Prophet's words for greeting those in their graves. Today's word.
screen: `THE GREETING TO THE DEAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: peace upon you, people of the graves. Say it once today, aloud or under your breath, when you think of someone who has died. Tomorrow, what continues. Day one thousand three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: When Muslims enter a graveyard, they greet the dead with the words the Prophet taught, beginning "as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar", and ask God's well-being and mercy for those buried there and for themselves.

options: why did you leave without telling me?

fork.reveal: in Sahih Muslim she asks what she should say to them, and he teaches her the greeting.

original.note: Arabic: peace be upon you, people of these dwellings.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims stand silently at graves.
what it means: they greet the dead with as-salamu 'alaykum, the same greeting they give the living, and ask well-being for both.
what a scholar hears: 'A'ishah's night at al-Baqi' and Buraydah's report, both in Sahih Muslim, calling the graves 'dwellings' and saying 'we will be joining you'.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 974 ('A'ishah follows the Prophet to al-Baqi'; what should I say to them?)

notes: Editor: hook corrected; in Muslim 974 'A'ishah sees him slip out and follows, so she 'can't find' him was inaccurate; he raised his hands three times, as the report says.
Muslim 974 and 975 paraphrased; confirm numbers and details of 'A'ishah's night account.
Arabic opening 'as-salamu 'alaykum ahl ad-diyar' given in transliteration and script; confirm vowels and the original-game pronunciation.
The index carry says 'people of the graves' while the hadith says 'dwellings'; the script explains 'dwellings'. Consider aligning the carry in the index.
'At the close of the prayer' refers to the taslim; confirm phrasing.
